wording: P89 finds that Liverpool English is characterised by low and rising contours: the most common phrase-final contour in Liverpool is L* L-H% (Knowles' 'rise'; 54% of tokens vs 7% in Manchester), with rise-plateau-slump used more by men (145 tokens, 34%) than women (48, 13%); Manchester uses mainly falls (H* L-L%), and very high final rises (possible HRT) were only six of 495 declaratives, all in Manchester. P89 argues the Liverpool rise came from new-dialect formation after rapid nineteenth-century growth (Lawton: 1349% in 1773-1871) with Irish input, a case where a minority variant was favoured.
locator: P89 Introduction to Conclusion, Tables 1-2, Figs. 2-6 (read in full)
counterevidence_limits: Read speech only; the historical account is argued, not tested. Slip: the text labels the Liverpool 'rise' L* H-H% in the results summary and in the Fig. 3 caption, although it defines L* H-H% as the 'rise-plateau' and tests L* L-H% as the most common Liverpool contour.
operationalization: HUM Ascendence = rising intonation in Liverpool English
verification_phrases: P89|L* L-H% represents what Knowles (1973) refers to as the || P89|phrase-final contours in Liverpool (L* H-H%) || P89|suggests a population increase of 1349%

wording: P89's statistics are internally consistent: every LRT p reproduces from its chi-square and df within 0.009 (largest gap: City x Gender in the nuclear model, 0.699 vs printed 0.69, within the rounding of chi-square 0.15), all '<0.001' entries are below 0.001; F0 gender chi2(1) 2.82 gives p 0.093; Lawton's 1349% follows from 34,500 to 500,000 (1349.3%); the rise-plateau-slump percentages imply about 47 tokens per male and 46 per female Liverpool speaker; the F0 means imply about 71 female of 138 values.
counterevidence_limits: Audits printed numbers only; the GLMMs were not refitted (data not used); equal token contribution per speaker is the agent's assumption.
